patient.name: Steven Achterberg
patient.chief_complaint: Painful bilateral leg cramps and progressive weakness for 10 months, family history of foot deformities
patient.hpi: Steven Achterberg is a 44-year-old building contractor presenting with a 10-month history of progressive bilateral leg weakness and painful cramps, predominantly in the calves. He has always been considered 'athletic but clumsy' and recalls childhood difficulty running fast and tripping over his own feet starting around age 8. He was told he had 'flat feet' as a child and wore orthotic insoles. He notes that his father and paternal uncle both had 'bad ankles' and trouble walking in their 50s, and his teenage son has started showing similar foot deformity. His current presentation is a noticeable worsening over the past year — he can no longer run at job sites and is developing difficulty climbing ladders. He has high-arched feet (pes cavus) and has always had hammer toes. He was evaluated by a podiatrist 5 years ago who attributed this to 'high arches.' He drinks 2-3 beers most nights. His HbA1c was checked last year at 5.4% (normal). He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. He has had no recent illness. He works in construction and uses power tools. On direct questioning, he reports that his hands have always been slightly weaker than peers ('always chose power tools over manual') and that he has had difficulty unscrewing caps. He has never been told he has a nerve problem.
pmh: Ankle sprain x2 in youth (attributed to coordination issues)
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: bilateral leg weakness and cramps, childhood foot deformities, family history of walking problems, teenage son developing similar feet. Negative: bowel/bladder dysfunction, rash, diabetes, hand weakness (subtle only), hearing loss.

family_history: Father: bilateral 'bad ankles,' required walking cane in his 50s, died at 62 (cardiac cause). Paternal uncle: similar gait problems, wheelchair-bound in 60s. Son (age 17): developing high-arched feet, referred to podiatrist. Mother: no neurological disease.

social_history.note: Building contractor, manual labor. Married. Regular alcohol — 2-3 beers most evenings (14-21 drinks per week — above recommended limits). Non-smoker. No illicit drugs. Construction work with power tools (noise exposure).

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II-XII intact. No facial weakness.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral foot drop: dorsiflexion 3/5 bilaterally, eversion 3/5 bilaterally. Plantar flexion 4/5 bilaterally. Intrinsic hand muscles (interossei): 4-/5 bilaterally. Wrist extensors 4+/5. Proximal lower extremity: hip flexors 4+/5, knee extensors 5/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced light touch and vibration in stocking distribution to mid-shin bilaterally (large fiber loss). Pinprick also mildly reduced bilateral feet. Vibration at great toes: 4 seconds bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 1+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 1+ bilaterally. Patellar 1+ bilaterally. Achilles: ABSENT bilaterally. All reflexes globally diminished.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild dysmetria on finger-nose bilaterally (hand intrinsic weakness contributing). Gait with bilateral high-steppage due to bilateral foot drop.
neurological_exam.gait: BILATERAL STEPPAGE GAIT. 'Stork leg' appearance — muscle wasting more prominent distally than proximally. Tandem walking markedly impaired. Inverted champagne bottle leg shape noted.
neurological_exam.special_tests: PES CAVUS bilaterally (arch height 42 mm — elevated). HAMMER TOES bilateral. Inverted champagne bottle appearance to calves (distal muscle wasting > proximal). No Babinski. No fasciculations.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: HbA1c 5.4 % (H), ALT 48 U/L (H), AST 52 U/L (H), GGT 88 U/L (H), MCV 92 fL (H).

report.summary: SEVERELY ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. Uniform, severely slowed conduction velocities throughout all motor nerves (30-35 m/s range) — classic CMT1 (demyelinating) pattern. Bilaterally symmetric involvement. NCS pattern is distinctly different from acquired neuropathy: uniformly slow, not focally slow with dispersion.

motor.flag: SEVERELY SLOW — amplitude also reduced (secondary axonal loss)

nerve_conduction_studies.note: KEY DISCRIMINATOR FROM CIDP: velocities uniformly slow throughout nerve (no focal slowing, no conduction block, no temporal dispersion). In CIDP, slowing is patchy and multifocal; in CMT1, slowing is uniform from root to terminal — 'global hypomyelination.'

muscles_tested.morphology: long-duration, high-amplitude, polyphasic — severe chronic reinnervation (giant MUPs)

emg.summary: Chronic secondary axonal loss with giant MUPs (evidence of decades of reinnervation) in distal muscles. Proximal muscles spared. Giant MUPs are characteristic of LONGSTANDING chronic neuropathy with decades of reinnervation — consistent with CMT onset in childhood.

report.overall_impression: HEREDITARY MOTOR AND SENSORY NEUROPATHY (CMT) PATTERN. Uniformly very slow conduction velocities (<38 m/s throughout all motor nerves, bilaterally symmetric) with giant MUPs on EMG indicating decades of reinnervation since childhood. This is CMT1 (demyelinating type) pattern. CIDP excluded by: symmetry, uniform slowing without conduction block/temporal dispersion, childhood onset, family history, absence of CSF protein elevation. GENETIC TESTING: PMP22 duplication (CMT1A — 70% of CMT1 cases) is first-line; also GJB1 (CMTX), MPZ. CRITICAL: alcohol superimposed on hereditary neuropathy can accelerate axonal loss — address alcohol use.

CMT Genetic Panel.value: POSITIVE — PMP22 gene duplication 17p11.2 confirmed by MLPA

output.procedure: Lumbar puncture — performed to exclude CIDP given demyelinating NCS pattern

results.citation: Leonardis L et al. (2012) Alcohol and CMT neuropathy: superimposed axonal damage. Muscle Nerve 46:604-609.
results.summary: Alcohol use in CMT patients causes superimposed axonal neuropathy on background hereditary demyelination; accelerates disability progression; GGT and liver enzymes often elevated; abstinence or significant reduction is recommended for all CMT patients.

output.interpretation: Alcohol use (14-21 drinks/week) in a CMT1A patient causes additive axonal neuropathy superimposed on the hereditary demyelinating background — this combination accelerates functional decline. GGT 88 U/L and AST elevation are alcohol markers. Alcohol reduction/abstinence is a modifiable factor that can slow progression. Refer for alcohol counseling and motivational interviewing. Brief intervention at this visit.

output.test_type: Sural Nerve Biopsy (deferred — not required given genetic confirmation)

report.summary: Sural nerve biopsy DEFERRED after PMP22 duplication confirmed genetically. When performed in CMT1A, biopsy would show: onion bulb formations (concentric Schwann cell wrapping around segmentally demyelinated axons), reduced myelinated fiber density, thinly myelinated fibers, normal or absent vasculitic change. With genetic confirmation, biopsy is not required and was not performed to spare patient an invasive procedure.
report.interpretation: Genetic confirmation of CMT1A makes nerve biopsy unnecessary. Biopsy is indicated in CMT only when genetic testing is non-diagnostic and hereditary vs acquired distinction is clinically critical.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A) — PMP22 duplication, with superimposed alcoholic neuropathy
critical_actions: Recognize uniformly slow NCS velocities (<38 m/s) as CMT pattern, not CIDP
CSF protein to distinguish CMT (normal) from CIDP (elevated) before unnecessary IVIG treatment
Order genetic panel (PMP22 duplication) — definitive diagnosis avoids invasive biopsy
Address alcohol — modifiable factor that superimposes axonal neuropathy on hereditary demyelination
Genetic counseling and family testing — autosomal dominant condition with 50% inheritance risk
contraindicated_actions: Do not treat with IVIG for presumed CIDP — CMT does not respond to immunotherapy; normal CSF protein excludes CIDP
Do not prescribe vincristine if patient ever requires chemotherapy — vincristine is contraindicated in CMT (causes acute fatal neuropathy)
Do not dismiss family history as coincidental — three-generation autosomal dominant pattern is CMT hallmark
Do not attribute all findings to alcohol — childhood onset and family history predate alcohol use

differential.key_distinguishing: CIDP: patchy, multifocal slowing with conduction block/temporal dispersion, elevated CSF protein, normal NCS at birth; CMT1A: uniformly slow velocities since birth, normal CSF protein, symmetric, autosomal dominant, no conduction block
Alcohol (14-21 drinks/week) causes axonal neuropathy superimposed on CMT; GGT elevated; alcohol alone would not explain pes cavus, childhood symptoms, family history, or uniformly slow NCS velocities
HbA1c 5.4% — no diabetes; diabetic neuropathy does not cause pes cavus or family history pattern

differential.condition: HNPP (hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies)
differential.key_distinguishing: HNPP: PMP22 DELETION (not duplication); presents with episodic focal pressure palsies; no progressive weakness; sausage-like myelin tomaculae on biopsy

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: Alcohol use history and regular drinker status is a significant anchoring trap toward purely alcoholic neuropathy
KEY DISCRIMINATOR: Childhood onset features (pes cavus since birth, 'clumsy' since age 8, hammer toes) are NOT explained by current alcohol use beginning in adulthood
FAMILY HISTORY spanning 3 generations is pathognomonic for autosomal dominant hereditary neuropathy — every neuropathy workup should include family history
NCS PATTERN: Uniform slow velocities (<38 m/s throughout, no focal areas of greater slowing) = hereditary CMT1 vs patchy multifocal slowing (CIDP)
CSF protein is the critical CIDP/CMT differentiator — CIDP always elevates CSF protein; hereditary neuropathy does not
Giant MUPs on EMG indicate decades of chronic reinnervation — acquired neuropathy 10 months duration would not produce giant MUPs
Alcohol superimposition: GGT elevated, AST elevated — alcohol causes additive axonal loss on top of hereditary demyelination; reduction is the only modifiable factor
